How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Psychedelic substances can profoundly alter the experience of time, yet we lack a detailed account of which distinct temporal alterations occur, how prevalent they are, and how they are interrelated. A key obstacle is that the methods best suited to capturing the phenomenological repertoire of altered temporality are difficult to scale and may therefore fail to reliably capture rare phenomena, whereas scalable psychometric tools lack the categorical resolution to tease apart distinct types of experience. Here we combine resolution with scale, applying a theorist-constructed phenomenological codebook to naturalistic psychedelic trip reports through large language model (LLM)based, corpus-scale content analysis. First, we establish that altered temporality resolves into seven textually distinguishable categories, recovered with similar reliability by human and LLM coders. Second, we apply LLM-based qualitative analysis to 3,291 excerpts from a corpus of 7,303 psychedelic trip reports, confirming that this categorical structure holds at corpus scale. Third, we estimate category prevalence and identify a stable associative structure comprising a complex of rare, interconnected alterations centered on timelessness and metaphysical appraisals, alongside an independent, more prevalent alteration in the subjective rate and duration of temporal flow. Fourth, we show that a similar relative prevalence profile and broad associative pattern, derived from the Englishlanguage Shroomery corpus, replicate in the independent Polish-language Neurogroove repository. Our study provides a high-resolution map of psychedelic temporality, arrived at by a method that may generalize beyond it, toward recovering the taxonomic structure of altered states of consciousness.

1. Introduction 1.1 Charting non-ordinary temporal experience and the methodological trade-off space

William James suggested that normal waking consciousness is only one special form of experience, separated "by the filmiest of screens" from other, entirely different forms (James, 1902 (James, /2012)). Contemporary consciousness science pursues a project of charting this wider space of experiential states beyond the ordinary baseline. This project consists of finding repeating patterns of altered experience, drawing categorical boundaries around them, and assembling from those categories a taxonomic map of non-ordinary consciousness. Here, we focus on a domain of non-ordinary phenomenology long recognized but never mapped in fine detail: the altered experience of time.

We contend that methods of charting non-ordinary phenomenology, including the temporal domain, must navigate a methodological trade-off space organized around three axes that pertain to (1) categorical resolution, (2) scale and coverage, and (3) epistemic proximity to experience.

The categorical resolution axis concerns the number of distinct, fine-grained, dissociable types of experience that a given charting instrument can register. Consider two such instruments: standardized psychometric questionnaires (Hood, 1975; Dittrich, 1998; Griffiths et al., 2006; Studerus et al., 2010; Studerus et al., 2011; MacLean et al., 2012; Barrett et al., 2015; Nour et al., 2016) and microphenomenological interview (as proposed in Petitmengin et al., 2019). Questionnaires offer relatively low categorical resolution: they rely on a limited number of items, where a single such item (such as MEQ's "loss of your usual sense of time") may lump together several potentially independent alterations into one score. By contrast, microphenomenological interviews -structured around guided reevocation of a specific episode -can elicit high-resolution descriptions of pre-reflective experience that psychometric instruments may not capture (Timmermann et al., 2025; Ermakova et al., 2025; Sanders et al., 2026).

The scale and coverage axis concerns the sample size a method can realistically reach, and thus its capacity to register rare types of experience. Applied to instruments mentioned above, this axis favors psychometric methods. Psychometric questionnaires have been deployed at scale in clinical trials and extended beyond laboratory settings with retrospective online surveys (Barrett et al., 2016; Carbonaro et al., 2016; Haijen et al., 2018; Griffiths et al., 2019; Davis et al., 2020). Microphenomenological interviews are more difficult to scale. The method demands intensive, guided vivisection of experience, which constrains existing studies to small samples and to short-acting compounds like intravenous DMT (Timmermann et al., 2025; Ermakova et al., 2025; Sanders et al., 2026).

The epistemic proximity axis concerns how directly the data reflect the original experience rather than its later reconstruction. Psychometric questionnaires are retrospective and sensitive to expectancy effects (dose and setting are verifiable in clinical trials, but not in online surveys). Microphenomenological interviews offer the closest available access, with almost immediate guided recall used to recover details before they are overwritten by constructive mnemonic processes or post-hoc interpretation. The advantage is a matter of degree, since evocation remains a reconstruction, and the interviewer's questions can shape recall.

Here, we propose an approach of mapping non-ordinary experience that aims to combine the advantages of high-resolution and large scale (we postpone the assessment of the method in light of the epistemic proximity axis until the Discussion section). The method applies a fine-grained, theorist-constructed taxonomic scheme to a corpus of thousands of unprompted first-person accounts of psychedelic experiences ("trip reports"), enabling the recovery of rare experiential categories.

Until recently, this kind of approach would have faced a cognitive bottleneck. Applying a detailed qualitative coding scheme to unstructured narratives is a demanding interpretive task. This, combined with the sheer volume of relevant corpora, makes exhaustive human coding practically unviable. However, corpus-scale analysis may be achievable with large language models (LLMs), provided their performance is not meaningfully inferior to that of competent human coders. Our approach therefore relies on deploying LLMs as artificial qualitative coders at corpus scale, but conditions the legitimacy of such deployment on an empirical non-inferiority assessment. Specifically, we employ preregistered non-inferiority criteria that LLM coders must meet against a human-validated reference sample before their output is used for substantive analysis (to be discussed in more detail in the Methods section). For the study, we deployed two LLMs that, at the outset of the project, constituted a state-of-the-art proprietary model (Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8) and a stateof-the-art open weights model (Z.ai's GLM 5.2).

This approach connects two strands of prior work on psychedelic experience reports.

Computational studies have analyzed large trip-report corpora using methods such as semantic-similarity analysis, topic modeling, linguistic-category word counts, and, more recently, LLM-based annotation (Sanz et al., 2018; Zamberlan et al., 2018; Martial et al., 2019; Ballentine et al., 2022; Bzdok et al., 2024; Noah et al., 2024; Žuljević et al., 2024), while human researchers have manually coded smaller bodies of text within qualitative designs (Brouwer et al., 2025; DellaCrosse et al., 2025; Dikovskaya et al., 2025; Schlomberg et al., 2026). Our approach uses LLMs to apply a high-resolution qualitative codebook at corpus scale. Thus, we aimed to reach the sample sizes of existing automated text analyses while retaining an explicit categorical instrument and a human reference standard.

1.2. A taxonomic map of altered time

To apply the method just outlined to the domain of altered temporal experience, we developed an extensive, hierarchically organized qualitative codebook (Table 1). The codebook proposes a categorical structure of the altered experiences of time, along with cognitive or reflective appraisals formed in response to such experiences, designed to recover and classify patterns present in unstructured first-person narratives. To explain its categorical structure, we will start by noting relatively invariant, structural elements of ordinary temporal experience, and then construe the codebook's taxonomic categories as representing ways in which those elements can dissolve or reorganize in an altered state (see also Shanon 2002, Ch. 14).

[Table 1 about here] Ordinary conscious experience involves the sense of the flow of time: an unceasing movement of becoming and fading, wherein what is anticipated continually materializes in the present, while the present recedes into the past. This felt passage proceeds at a relatively bounded pace, and experienced durations approximately track objective intervals. In the psychedelic state, this rate of flow or perceived duration can be radically distorted (main code RTD): temporal flow may feel decelerated or accelerated far beyond ordinary bounds (subcode rtd.rat), and subjective temporal intervals can radically expand or compress (subcode rtd.dur).

The ordinary sense of temporal flow also exhibits a linear progression (the subjective "arrow of time"), with successive experiences coalescing into a coherent, forward-directed stream. In the psychedelic experience, this topological structure can fracture (main code STF): experienced temporal succession may reverse (subcode stf.rev), shatter into disjointed, scrambled fragments (subcode stf.dso), or fold back on itself into recursive temporal loops (subcode stf.lop).

In the ordinary baseline case, subjects possess a sense of apprehending the world from a situated location in time -a temporal vantage point anchored in a "present moment" that can be positioned on an autobiographical or historical scale. In the psychedelic state, this standpoint can decouple from the objective present (main code REL). Subjects may experience being relocated to a different autobiographical or historical era (subcode rel.trv), or feel situated at two distinct temporal points simultaneously (subcode rel.bil).

In ordinary experience, the baseline features discussed above constitute an invariant, pervasive phenomenological structure. In the psychedelic state, this structure can not only become disorganized or reorganized, but dissolve altogether, producing an experience of timelessness (main code TLS). Drawing on work in philosophy (Gładziejewski, 2026) The ordinary state also includes the recognition of being embedded within an extended autobiographical narrative and a shared intersubjective world. In psychedelic states, this narrative and social orientation can reconfigure (main code NSO). At the autobiographical level, subjects may radically re-evaluate their life trajectory, confront their mortality, or experience their future horizon as opening anew or foreclosing (subcode nso.nar). At the interpersonal level, the sense of participating in shared social time can alter (subcode nso.soc), ranging from deep, communion-like temporal synchronization with companions to the feeling of being desynchronized and trapped in an isolated temporal bubble.

Finally, in everyday life, time serves as an intuitive, practically indispensable category that structures action and organizes daily concerns. In the psychedelic state, this framework can collapse into a loss of the meaning of time (main code LMG). This breakdown can manifest as conceptual dissolution, wherein the very idea of time, temporal order, or clock measures ceases to be intelligible (subcode lmg.cnc), or as evaluative insignificance, with time and temporal distinctions ceasing to matter, appraised as irrelevant or inconsequential (subcode lmg.ins).

2. Methods

>Methods

2.1 Study design overview

The study design (Fig. 1) comprises four main parts. First, an LLM-based, high-recall filter is used to identify reports likely to convey temporal experience along with its appraisals, and to extract relevant, source-verbatim passages. Second, a qualitative codebook is iteratively developed and frozen for coding. Third, the codebook is applied independently by two LLM coders to filtered excerpts. The results are used to identify rare codes and mechanically construct a rare-code-enriched reliability sample for human coders. Fourth, conditional on the LLM coding reliability being established as non-inferior to human coding, full-corpus descriptive and association analyses are performed on the complete LLM-coding datasets.

[Figure 1 about here]

2.2 Data extraction and substance classification

The primary corpus was the trip-report archive of Shroomery.org, an anonymous psilocybin mushroom-focused forum established in 1997. Reports are unprompted firstperson narratives, not linked to any author-identifying information. Content in the Shroomery corpus is made available under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license, permitting noncommercial reuse and adaptation with appropriate attribution. The site's trip report repository records no separate substance or dose field, but this information is usually reported in the report title or free-text body, and experiences are assigned to one of five user-assigned intensity tiers. All reports were retrieved following the collection procedure of Žuljević et al. (2024), at one request per second in accordance with the site's robots directive. Data cleanup removed entries under 50 verified English words and duplicates, leaving a corpus of 7,303 reports.

A deterministic classifier, validated against the raw substance text, then partitioned reports into pharmacological categories based on the substance reported. The main analysis sample covered only the reports describing a classic serotonergic (5-HT2Aagonist) psychedelic experience, alone or with common adjuncts, which we considered as having negligible or merely modulating (dampening or intensifying) effect on core psychedelic phenomenology (cannabis, alcohol, tobacco, inert additions, or MAOI potentiators). The cannabis-involving reports were retained, with the plan to test the possible confounding influence of cannabis on temporal experience in later analysis.

Excluded from the analysis were reports involving a psychedelic along with a phenomenology-altering co-drug (295 reports), experiences occasioned by substances that are not serotonergic psychedelics (113), and reports with unspecified substances (114). Hence, the corpus contains 6,781 reports that are congruent with the substanceeligibility rule of this study.

2.3 Filtering and unit construction

To make subsequent coding computationally and cognitively manageable, each remaining report was screened independently by Claude Opus 4.8 (one fresh, stateless single-turn agent per report, run headless through Anthropic's command-line harness with tool use disabled) and GLM-5.2 (one fresh, stateless API call per report at temperature 0, tool use disabled), using a shared frozen prompt. The prompt was designed to remain generic and theoretically neutral, not referring to categories used in the codebook, and instead asking the model to include the report if it contained "changes or alterations in the experience of time, or the temporal structure of experience" or "cognitive/affective appraisals of time, or beliefs or insights about time". The prompt also asked the model to discount temporal information related to scene setting, narrative timestamps or bare clock-time duration statements. The filter design favored recall over precision, as remaining reports lacking interesting temporal-experience content could be flagged as such during coding.

Each model returned (1) an include/exclude decision with a confidence rating (high/medium/low), and, for an included report, (2) the relevant passages cited as whole sentences. The two model votes were combined with a decision rule: two includes produced an automatic include; two excludes produced an automatic exclude; a high-or medium-confidence include paired with an exclude produced an automatic include; a lowconfidence include paired with a low-confidence exclude produced an automatic include; a low-confidence include paired with an exclude was human-adjudicated when the other model's exclusion was high or medium.

Model agreement rose monotonically with the stated confidence of decision, reaching overall κ = 0.903. Human adjudication covered 267 model-contested reports, so ~96% of the corpus was decided automatically. Of those adjudicated, only 16 reports were included. The procedure yielded 3,291 included reports (48.53% of the substancecongruent part of the whole Shroomery corpus).

A mechanical verbatim verification required every passage selected by a model as conveying relevant content to be a literal substring of the source report. Any discrepancies were detected and manually corrected. Where both models decided to include a report, they pointed at highly overlapping fragments (median character-level Jaccard = 1.00).

As an additional extraction recall audit, the included reports were deterministically segmented into sentences, and each sentence had the filter individually applied to it by a third model (Sonnet 5, Anthropic) under a rule that a sentence is added to existing excerpts if it is judged relevant with high certainty on two independent runs. This added sentences to 854 of the 3,291 excerpts, and the recovered material accounts for 22.2% of the sentences in the coded corpus (two-thirds of those continue a passage the original filter had already selected, effectively expanding context). A 150-report human audit of double-included reports (a stratified set, over-sampling reports with below Jaccard = 0.5 overlap on the initial Opus-GLM run) found no major missing relevant fragments. All the fragments selected, with string overlaps removed, were joined to construct the final units on which coding was performed.

2.4 Codebook development

The codebook design process was predominantly theory-driven, inspired by seminal work on psychedelic phenomenology (Shanon, 2002, chap. 14), as well as recent philosophical research on psychedelic temporal experience (Gładziejewski, 2026; Miceli McMillan et al., 2025). An additional theoretical source was work on temporal experience and ideation in clinical contexts (Whiteley, 2025; Kusters, 2020; Moskalewicz & Schwartz, 2020; Fuchs, 2013; Ratcliffe, 2012). Some codes were developed inductively, through informal reading of the corpus reports (in particular, the "loss of meaning" code with its subcodes and the "absence of time" as a separate subcode of "timelessness"). Following a preliminary human coding round on 90 reports, a decision was made to introduce a hierarchical codesubcode structure at two levels of conceptual granularity. The codebook was then frozen as version 1.0 before any production coding. The human and LLM coders used byteidentical copies of the instrument, verified against its SHA-256 hash. No codebook category or definition was modified during the human or LLM coding rounds.

2.5 Qualitative Coding

LLM coding was designed to mirror the human coding process (described below). Each unit is coded by one fresh, stateless model instance (Opus 4.8, GLM 5.2, settings matching the filtering run) in a single turn with no tool access. Each model coded all 3,291 units under dated model builds, with the model identity verified per call and a completion check requiring every unit to be coded by both models before aggregation. In this process, a model instance sees the codebook and the unit's excerpts. A model may open the full source report to resolve ambiguity only on request, which is logged. Its output format matches exactly the human tool's output, including an "other" flag for potentially relevant phenomena the codebook does not cover. The model may fill a per-unit note defined as an uncertainty tracker, where it is asked to flag hesitations on using a code and deliberations between alternative codes that could interpret the material. Every assigned code carries a verbatim evidence quote that is mechanically verified against the source.

Agreement and prevalence outputs were generated but masked from the members of the research team who participated in the human coding round.

The human reliability sample was assembled by a fully mechanical, seeded sampler over the two LLM code matrices. The process was designed to ensure that the human reliability sample is enriched for rare codes. One draw based on predefined rules was performed, with no later additions. The sample, comprising 247 units, comprised five types of components: • a natural-prevalence component: 100 units selected by uniform seeded sampling from the full corpus; • near-extinct-code census: all units positive for any subcode whose full-corpus prevalence was at or below its sampling floor: ≤30 units for a main code or ≤20 for a subcode; • reliability enrichment component: for codes above the near-extinct threshold, additional units were selected until the sample contained at least 30 instances of each main code and 20 instances of each subcode; • disagreement enrichment component: for every main code and subcode, the sample was required to contain at least five units on which the two models disagreed; • recall probes: for each main code with a prevalence below 50%, five additional units were selected that neither model coded positive: (1) two semantic-neighbor probes, chosen by cosine similarity to an anchor set of both-model positively coded examples (mixedbread-ai/mxbai-embed-large-v1 sentence-embedding model was used); (2) three notes probes, sampled from units where the code was mentioned in both models' free-text uncertainty trackers despite neither model eventually assigning the code.

The draw ran from hash-frozen inputs, executed and supervised by team members who did not participate in the human coding round. Human coders received only unit identifiers and text. Because the sample over-represents disputed and rare units by design, it is used only for reliability and non-inferiority estimation, with prevalence estimated on the full-corpus matrices, under the condition that preregistered criteria of LLM reliability are met.

Human coding. Three humans, identified here as H1-H3, applied the codebook to the reliability sample. One of them was blind to the study hypotheses and did not belong to the research team. This person received a walkthrough of the codebook, a practice round on 36 synthetic units containing planted lures (platitudes that the codebook explicitly asks not to code), and a decision-threshold calibration round based on inspecting examples of expert-consensus code applications (with research team members treated as experts).

The coding process used a custom instrument: a self-contained HTML file per coder, embedding the frozen codebook, the units and their full source reports. The coding procedure employed the same protocol as in the case of LLM coders. Full reports were opened only to settle a decision in ambiguous cases and a per-unit notebook was available to note hesitations and competing interpretations.

2.6 Cross-linguistic generalization: the Polish Neurogroove corpus

The same frozen codebook and the same two LLM coders were applied to an independent corpus, Neurogroove (neurogroove.info). NeuroGroove is the trip-report archive of hyperreal.info, a Polish drug-education community online since 1996, with trip reports recovered for this study spanning from 1999 to 2026. The site's content is published under the CC BY-SA 4.0 license. Report extraction respected the site's robots directive. Of the 3,129 reports scraped, 885 were left as substance-eligible under the same classification scheme as the one used for the Shroomery corpus.

The process of filtering reports for potentially relevant content was a streamlined version of the Shroomery scheme, with GLM 5.2 filtering omitted for the reports Opus 4.8 had already included at high or medium confidence, where a second vote could not change the outcome under the decision rule. Sonnet-5-based excerpt enrichment and final coding-unit construction were performed the same way as with the Shroomery corpus.

The LLM coding process performed on the Neurogroove corpus matched the one employed in the Shroomery case. Both LLMs coded the final, filtered set of 542 units (61.2% of all substance-eligible reports in this corpus).

2.7 Analysis conventions

Measures and data processing. Gwet's AC1 (Gwet, 2008) is the preregistered primary agreement measure. The choice follows from the fact (anticipated following the initial inspection of the filtered dataset) that the corpus, even after applying the filter, is strongly dominated by negative judgments for most codes. Under low prevalence, Cohen's κ is systematically decreased by its chance-correction term even where raw agreement is near-perfect (the kappa paradox; Feinstein & Cicchetti, 1990). AC1 is more robust to skewed marginals (Gwet, 2008; Wongpakaran et al., 2013), so the study hypotheses are evaluated against it. Cohen's κ, positive agreement and overall agreement are reported alongside as descriptive context, with Krippendorff's α per coder pool reported as the multi-coder generalization. All deterministic data processing, statistical analysis (including Gwet's AC1, Cohen's κ, Krippendorff's α, odds ratios, Fisher's exact tests, FDR correction, bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests), as well as figure generation were performed with Python scripts developed for this study. The computational layer used only the Python standard library. Frozen JSON, JSONL, and CSV input files were recorded in SHA-256 manifests and checked for file drift before analysis. Analytic results were written to JSON files, from which the report tables and figures were generated. These scripts were written with the assistance of a large language model (Claude Fable, Anthropic), and all code was reviewed and verified by the authors.

Preregistered hypothesis evaluation criteria.

This study is a part of a research project preregistered on OSF, with the present paper covering hypothesis 1 and 2 stated in the preregistration. The registration is publicly available at https://osf.io/de2a5. Preregistered Hypothesis 1 predicts, for each of the seven main codes, AC1 agreement of at least 0.70 (0.80 for strong confirmation) independently within human-human pairs and within the cross-model LLM pairs, along with a saturation condition, where the residual "other" flag (indicating a presence of study-relevant phenomenon that does not fit any existing code) is raised on no more than 10% of reliability-sample units. For the preregistered Hypothesis 2, the condition is that, per main code, (1) the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval on ΔAC1 = mean human-human minus mean LLM-human must fall below +0.10, and (2) LLM-human agreement must clear a threshold of 0.70 AC1. For the latter criterion, mean pairwise LLM-human AC1 was used as a measure. Results bearing on the preregistered hypotheses are presented for the seven main codes, whereas the whole-corpus prevalence and inter-model agreement tables additionally include subcode-level estimates, which are treated here as exploratory.

3. Results

>Results

3.1 Evaluation of codebook reliability

The preregistered weak-confirmation criterion of hypothesis 1 is met, with every humanhuman pair and the LLM-LLM pair for every main code above AC1 0.70. Mean per-code LLM-human AC1, reported here as additional evidence, is also above 0.70 for every code (Table 2). At the level of the group summaries shown in Table 2, six out of seven main codes have AC1 above 0.80 for mean human-human, mean LLM-human and LLM-LLM agreement. RTD is the exception, with mean human-human (0.761), mean LLM-human (0.724) and LLM-LLM (0.776) AC1 below 0.80. Out of all 70 individual pairwise per-code AC1 agreement measurements (7 main codes × 10 coder pairs: three human-human, six LLMhuman, one LLM-LLM), only one LLM-human pair sits below AC1 0.70: an RTD pair at 0.687 (Figure 2). The preregistered saturation condition is also met, with the highest human other-flag rate at 5.7%.

[Table 2 about here]

In the case of six main codes (RTD, STF, REL, TLS, MPH, LMG), the secondary agreement measures convergently support their reliable applicability in the coding task. For these codes, all group-mean and LLM-LLM Cohen's κ values fall within or above Landis and Koch's (1977) "substantial" agreement band (0.61-0.80), while positive and overall agreement exceed 0.75. The NSO code diverges from this pattern, despite it comfortably reaching the AC1 criterion. Krippendorff's α (nominal) generalizes chance-corrected agreement to any number of coders. Its values lie close to κ at every pool: over the three human coders α per main code is RTD 0.75, STF 0.74, REL 0.77, TLS 0.67, MPH 0.74, NSO 0.57, LMG 0.74; pooled over all five coders it is 0.73, 0.73, 0.77, 0.72, 0.74, 0.57, 0.77 in the same order; the LLM pair spans 0.56-0.84.

NSO is systematically lower than other main codes specifically on κ (0.559-0.581), positive agreement (0.615-0.634) and Krippendorff's α (0.56-0.57). We do not consider these values disqualifying this code as reliable, given the difficulty of the task, but we note that NSO shows weaker agreement under the mentioned secondary measures.

[Figure 2 about here]

3.2 Evaluation of LLM-coder non-inferiority to human coders

Both preregistered conditions of hypothesis 2 are met for all seven main codes. For the non-inferiority condition, the upper bound of the paired-bootstrap 95% CI remains below the +0.10 margin for every code (Figure 3). ΔAC1 is defined as mean human-human minus mean LLM-human agreement, so negative values indicate higher LLM-human agreement.

It ranges from -0.047 (TLS) to 0.037 (RTD): LLM-human agreement is higher for STF, REL, TLS and LMG, effectively equal to human-human agreement for NSO, and slightly lower for RTD and MPH.

For the absolute-agreement condition, mean LLM-human AC1 ranges from 0.724 to 0.934 and therefore exceeds 0.70 for every code (Table 2). RTD has the lowest mean LLM-human AC1 (0.724). As noted in Section 3.1, one of its six individual LLM-human pairs falls below 0.70 (AC1 = 0.687). RTD therefore passes under the adopted mean-floor interpretation of the preregistered criterion (we note that it would not pass the stricter sensitivity interpretation requiring every individual pair to reach 0.70).

[Figure 3 about here]

3.3 Whole corpus analysis: inter-model agreement and code prevalences

Corpus-scale inter-model agreement is high across all seven main codes (Table 3). AC1 ranges from 0.771 to 0.986 and overall agreement from 0.878 to 0.986; κ ranges from 0.633 to 0.802 and positive agreement from 0.655 to 0.836. The corpus-scale measures broadly reproduce the LLM-LLM agreement profile observed in the 247-unit validation sample: agreement remains consistently high across codes, with RTD again the lowest on AC1. This continuity shows that the inter-model reliability pattern scales to the full 3,291unit corpus rather than being artificially enforced by the composition of the validation sample. NSO again produces the lowest κ and positive agreement despite high AC1 and overall agreement, reproducing the validation-sample pattern and indicating that agreement on positive NSO assignments is weaker than its high AC1 and raw agreement alone would suggest.

[Table 3 about here] Table 4 shows broadly similar prevalence rankings across the two models. RTD is by far the most frequently assigned main code, occurring in 38.68% of filtered units for Opus 4.8 and 35.76% for GLM 5.2. All other main codes occur in 2.77-9.05% of units according to Opus and 3.28-12.58% according to GLM. GLM is the more liberal coder than Opus on non-RTD codes, with the largest difference for TLS (12.58% versus 9.05%). Opus assigns RTD more often (38.68% versus 35.76%). The within-code subcode profiles are consistent across models.

[Table 4 about here] Because cannabis independently alters time perception (Atakan et al., 2012; Sewell et al., 2013), a systematically shifted temporal experience profile among cannabis-involving reports would mean that their inclusion was distorting the prevalence attributed here to psychedelic experiences. We found no evidence of such distortion. Cannabis-involving and pure-psychedelic reports had nearly identical code rankings (ρ = .964), with lower REL the only recurring difference (RR = 0.51/0.57; q = .030/.052). Cannabis-involving and other psychedelic-involving combinations (of those that met the substance inclusion criteria of this study) differed on no main code after FDR correction, although REL was again less prevalent with cannabis (RR = 0.36/0.47; q = .063/.333). Cannabis also does not behave as the general experience-intensifier it is sometimes taken to be in psychedelic communities (at least not in the temporal domain), as only two of seven main codes were more prevalent in cannabis-involving than in pure-psychedelic reports. Across all seven codes, the geometric mean of the code-specific RRs was 0.87/0.89

3.4 The co-occurrence complex and the independence of rate and duration distortion

To examine how the associative structure of the seven main codes was organized across reports, we estimated all 21 pairwise associations separately in each full-corpus LLM coding matrix (N = 3,291). Odds ratios were calculated from unconditional 2 × 2 tables, with Fisher's exact tests and BH-FDR correction across the 21 pairs per model. Before interpreting individual associations, we assessed whether the two coders recovered the same overall structure. Their 21 log odds ratios were strongly correlated (Spearman's ρ = .944, permutation p < .001), with agreement on the direction of 20 of 21 associations.

Concordance remained high after excluding the six RTD pairs (ρ = .868, p < .001). Overall, the resulting association structure is convergent across both models used.

Nine positive associations survived FDR correction in both models, eight of which also survived Bonferroni correction in both. Together, they formed a single connected component linking three alterations of immediate temporal experience -structure of flow (STF), relocation of standpoint (REL), and timelessness (TLS) -with metaphysical insight (MPH), narrative and social orientation (NSO), and loss of meaning (LMG; Fig. 4a). The replicated associations had odds ratios of 2.0-4.3. The strongest edges linked TLS with MPH (OR = 4.31/3.35, Opus/GLM) and MPH with NSO (OR = 4.20/3.78), positioning MPH as a hub between altered temporal experience and its appraisal. By contrast, RTD -the most prevalent code -had no replicated association with another code. Its odds ratios ranged from 0.62 to 1.37, were mostly non-significant, and showed no consistent direction across coders, indicating approximate independence from the six-code complex.

[Figure 4 about here]

We investigated whether the co-occurrence complex could be explained by an experienceintensity gradient, where more intense experiences simply contain more codable phenomena. Each of the nine associations was re-estimated within the Shroomery's five self-rated intensity tiers and pooled using Mantel-Haenszel estimators, with 2,000replicate unit-level bootstrap confidence intervals. All nine associations remained positive in both coding matrices. Adjusted odds ratios ranged from 1.76 to 3.81, and every confidence interval excluded 1. Conditioning reduced the log odds ratios by 3-36%, but preserved their ordering, with TLS-MPH and MPH-NSO remaining among the strongest associations. The complex therefore cannot be attributed solely to experience intensity, although residual confounding by dimensions not captured by the five-level rating remains possible. Similar reasoning applies to report length. Re-estimating the same nine associations within word-count octiles of the source reports and pooling as above left all nine positive in both coding matrices, with adjusted odds ratios of 1.77-3.83 and every confidence interval excluding 1. Conditioning on length reduced the log odds ratios by 2-26%, so length accounted for part of each association but not for the complex itself.

Finally, we examined the stability of this associative pattern across the Shroomery archive's calendar history, using recovered publication dates for all source reports. The coded units were divided into three equal-count periods, and the associations were reestimated within each period (Fig. 4b). Of the 27 complex-edge × period point estimates, 26 were above OR = 1 for Opus and all 27 for GLM. Across all three periods, RTD associations remained comparatively close to independence, with point estimates on either side of OR = 1. The distinction between the co-occurrence complex and approximately independent RTD therefore persisted across historical variation in the Shroomery corpus.

3.5 Cross-linguistic generalization: code prevalence, associative structure, and inter-model agreement

The principal patterns identified in Shroomery are replicated in the Polish Neurogroove corpus: the inter-model agreement profile and relative code prevalences were closely preserved, and the co-occurrence complex reappeared wherever the smaller trip repository provided sufficient support for estimation.

Inter-model agreement remained high when the same two coders and frozen instrument were applied to Neurogroove (Table 5). Across the seven main codes, AC1 ranged from .833 to .986, Cohen's κ from .688 to .847, positive agreement from .729 to .892, and overall (raw) agreement from .913 to .987. These ranges closely reproduced the Shroomery profile reported in Table 3 (AC1 = .771-.986, κ = .633-.802, positive agreement = .655-.836, overall agreement = .878-.986).

[Table 5 about here]

The prevalence profile also translated across corpora (Fig. 5a). RTD remained by far the most frequent code, TLS ranked second, and REL remained rare in both coding matrices.

Correlations between the corpora's seven-code prevalence ranks were .89-.96 across coder comparisons. Neurogroove showed higher per-unit prevalence for most codes.

Neurogroove's reports are ~1.6x longer than Shroomery's (median 1,122 vs 714 words) and this accounted for part of this difference: standardizing Shroomery to Neurogroove's report-length distribution brought RTD, LMG, and REL approximately to parity, whereas higher Neurogroove prevalence remained most evident for TLS, MPH, and NSO, and more mildly for STF. The same pattern held when prevalence was computed over all substancecongruent reports rather than coded units, with filter-excluded reports counted as codenegative (N = 6,781 and 885).

The co-occurrence structure was reproduced where Neurogroove contained enough observations to estimate it reliably (Fig. 5b). We treated a code pair as measurable only when each of the four coder-corpus matrices contained at least five reports positive for both codes. Sixteen of the 21 possible pairs met this threshold. All five excluded pairs involved REL. Across the 16 measurable pairs, same-coder Shroomery-Neurogroove estimates had mean absolute log-odds-ratio differences of .35 for Opus and .30 for GLM, with matching directions for 12/16 and 10/16 pairs, respectively; rank-order correlations were ρ = .75 (permutation p = .002) and ρ = .63 (p = .010). Of the nine edges defining the Shroomery complex, six were measurable in Neurogroove, and every one was positive for both coders (ORs = 1.3-4.2). The other three complex edges all involved REL and therefore remained untested rather than failing to replicate. Meanwhile, the six measurable RTD associations continued to fall on both sides of OR = 1, reproducing RTD's separation from the complex.

[Figure 5 about here]

We note a limitation of the cross-linguistic generalization. Although visual inspection of LLM behavior on the Neurogroove corpus did not raise doubts about their performance as coders, systematic human coding validation was conducted only on the English-language Shroomery corpus. The reported Neurogroove reliability therefore rests on inter-model agreement between two independently trained LLMs, which does not exclude the possibility of concordant error (both models misapplying a code in the same direction on Polish-language material).

4. Discussion

>Discussion

4.1. Summary: a high-resolution map of psychedelic temporality

In this study, we produced a high-resolution taxonomic map of psychedelic temporality, using a method that combines scale with fine-grained phenomenological coding. We also showed that the map applies to two separate trip report corpora, written in different languages, and coming from distinct online communities. The findings establish that widespread alterations in the rate and duration of time dissociate from a rarer, mutually associated complex centered on the experience of timelessness and metaphysical appraisals. By reliably recovering these rare experiential structures at scale, the approach proves that LLM-based qualitative coding can overcome the traditional bottleneck of human textual analysis.

We note that this method yields the categorical resolution required to separate distinct experiential phenomena that standard psychometric questionnaires have historically collapsed into single items. In the widely used Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ30), for instance, the item "loss of your usual sense of time" could be equally satisfied by changes in subjective speed or duration (RTD code), disordered temporal structure (STF), the loss of temporal significance (LMG), or the total vanishing of time (TLS). Our study shows these states are distinct. Similarly, MEQ30's item assessing a "sense of being 'outside of' time, beyond past and future" arguably collapses what our study reveals as three distinct modes of timelessness: time simply vanishing as a dimension of awareness (tls.abs subcode), a frozen present that no longer flows (tls.nop), and the simultaneous apprehension of all events (tls.etr).

The value of this granularity may extend beyond a purely descriptive or taxonomic one.

Research indicates that individual items and distinct facets within mystical experience scales differentially predict therapeutic efficacy and mental health outcomes (Roseman et al., 2018). By further teasing apart what questionnaires lump together, a high-resolution map like the one recovered here could allow clinical researchers to test which precise phenomenological variants are driving positive psychological change. Categorical granularity is therefore not merely a taxonomic virtue, but could deepen our understanding of the experiential underpinnings of psychedelic therapy.

4.2. Mechanistic dissociation hypothesis

The method employed in this study is, at its core, a way of finding dissociable types of experience in textual data. This in turn can inform and inspire hypotheses about the mechanisms underlying such experiential patterns. Consider the code association structure the present study uncovered. One mechanistic view of psychedelic temporality relies on interval-timing models which propose that internally generated pulses pass through an attention-dependent gate into an accumulator, with the resulting count compared against duration representations held in memory (Treisman, 1963; Gibbon et al., 1984). Psychedelic-induced temporal disturbance can be located downstream of the pacemaker: when attention is drawn away from time, fewer pulses may be registered, while demands on working memory may compromise the maintenance of the duration representation against which the accumulated quantity is compared (Wittmann et al., 2007; see also Wackermann et al., 2008). Such accounts provide natural candidate explanations for what the present study identified as altered rate and duration of subjective time (RTD): experiences in which temporal succession remains intact, but its apparent pace or metric is altered.

A tempting extension of this account is that more radical departures from ordinary temporality arise when distortions of temporal rate or duration reach an extreme.

Consistent with this possibility, Shanon describes an ayahuasca-induced experiential trajectory in which alterations in the rate of subjective time culminate in the stopping of time or a sense of being outside time (2002, pp. 229, 231). Although he argues that the resulting atemporality can no longer be adequately characterized as rate distortion alone (pp. 234-235), the trajectory he describes places RTD and timelessness at successive stages of a single experiential progression. The present findings suggest an alternative hypothesis: rather than constituting progressively more radical expressions of one underlying disturbance, RTD and the alterations belonging to the association complex may depend on partially dissociable neural or computational mechanisms. RTD was by far the most prevalent category, yet it sat outside the code association complex. By contrast, the complex itself comprises less prevalent disturbances of temporal structure and standpoint, including timelessness, along with cognitive appraisals of time (Figure 4). One possibility, therefore, is that disruptions of interval timing, temporal attention, or duration estimation principally contribute to RTD, whereas the association complex depends on a distinct mechanism (or set of mechanisms). The code association structure cannot justify this kind of account by itself, but it invites considering mechanistic dissociation as a hypothesis worth testing.

4.3. Why narrative and social temporality were harder to measure

In sections 3.1 and 3.3, we noted NSO (appraisals of time at the narrative and social level) as the main code that needs a separate treatment. It met the preregistered AC1 criterion and the LLM non-inferiority criterion, and overall agreement on using this code remained high. Yet it was the clear outlier on measures sensitive to agreement about positive cases: across the three coder-group comparisons, Cohen's κ was 0.56-0.58 and positive agreement was 0.62-0.63, the lowest values for any main code. Krippendorff's α likewise placed NSO at the floor of every coder pool. The same pattern of lower agreement was repeated at the inter-model corpus-scale comparison. We do not treat this as evidence that NSO failed completely as a category, since a clear majority of positive assignments were shared. However, it does show that NSO's boundary was more fuzzy than those of the other six codes.

An additional filter audit located the same difficulty one processing stage earlier. We screened 200 randomly selected reports that had been excluded by the high-recall filter, using Opus 4.8 to assess the seven main codes. None of the other six codes was detected on that run, providing a positive check on the filter's recall for the study's core categories.

NSO, however, was identified in five reports (2.5%), roughly half its 5.3% prevalence among the filter-included reports coded by the same LLM. This indicates that NSO does not align cleanly with the liberal boundary used by the filter.

To put this weakness in context, we need to consider the motivation behind introducing NSO to the codebook. The code was included to test whether psychedelic temporality transforms some of the same dimensions used by modern phenomenologists to characterize depressive temporality. Fuchs (2013) describes depression through inhibited affective-conative momentum (the future loses its affective pull on a subject) and desynchronization from socially shared time. Ratcliffe (2012) similarly emphasizes a collapse of practical significance and meaningful future possibilities. Drawing on this work, Miceli McMillan et al. (2025) propose psychedelic temporality as a counterweight to this closure, which could explain therapeutic benefits of psychedelic use for depression (see also Whiteley, 2025). Thus, NSO was designed to seek textual traces of a pattern where the past becomes less binding, the future regains its affective pull, or a person regains their sense of being in sync with the time of others.

However, it appears that such subtle, tacit structures of temporality are not easy to pinpoint textually in the naturalistic corpora analyzed here. Most trip reports are not carefully structured phenomenological descriptions. In such texts, the themes that NSO was designed to recover often appear in passages that are not explicitly focused on expressing temporal contents. A filter centered on overt temporal themes may therefore miss them. The filter leakage and weaker positive agreement may thus reflect the same construct-instrument mismatch. NSO remains, we contend, theoretically well-motivated, but its results warrant greater caution and subsequent validation with other methods, like phenomenological interview.

4.4. Naturalistic trip reports and the epistemic proximity axis

In the introduction, we listed epistemic proximity to experience as one of the three axes of the methodological trade-off space which must be navigated by distinct approaches to taxonomizing non-ordinary consciousness. While the approach we employed here combines scale with high categorical resolution, it is considerably more limited when it comes to epistemic proximity. Naturalistic trip reports lack control and objective verification regarding substance identity, dosage, and setting. No standardized protocols for report writing and structuring are used. Because authors write without structured phenomenological guidance, the resulting corpus indiscriminately juxtaposes high-effort, detailed introspective narratives with crude, fragmented, low-effort accounts. The interval between the experience and its reconstruction is entirely unconstrained: observations recorded immediately following the experience are mixed with reports written weeks or months after the event, leaving the data susceptible to recall decay and reconstructive memory distortions.

However, two considerations indicate how this limitation can be compensated for. First, the method used in the present study is meant to recover robust high-level patterns in text. It registers the presence of a category provided it reliably recurs across a large body of individual reports. Hence, the noisiness of individual reports is largely attenuated in the process, as the method works by homing in on corpus-scale narrative or semantic regularities. Furthermore, such regularities are robust in that they are convergently recovered by multiple interpreters and across separate corpora produced by linguistically distinct communities.

Second, the approach employed here is not a self-standing alternative to standardized questionnaires or phenomenological interviews. All three should be considered components of an integrated methodological toolkit. No single method can simultaneously maximize phenomenological resolution, empirical scale, and epistemic proximity. Navigating the trade-off space effectively requires triangulation, where the weaknesses of one approach are counterbalanced by the strengths of another. Within such an undertaking, corpus-scale qualitative coding serves as a discovery engine. Finegrained categories identified across thousands of spontaneous accounts can be incorporated into new, higher-resolution psychometric items and targeted interview protocols. In this way, standardized instruments gain conceptual granularity, while phenomenological patterns discovered in naturalistic texts become systematically testable under more controllable conditions.

5. Conclusion

In this study, we have charted the structure of altered temporal experience under psychedelics, using a human-validated, LLM-assisted method to recover phenomenological patterns from naturalistic trip reports accumulated online over decades. The resulting map, replicated across two distinct corpora, reveals that common changes in the subjective rate and duration of time stand apart from a co-associated complex of rarer alterations centered on timelessness and the appraisals that accompany it. The approach is not specific to temporality, and it may generalize to other domains of altered experience. Combined with questionnaires and interview-based methods, it offers Table 2. , the codebook distinguishes different forms of such dissolution: time itself may simply vanish as an experiential dimension (subcode tls.abs); temporal flow may come to a standstill, leaving only an unmoving present moment (subcode tls.nop); or the situated temporal vantage point may collapse into a state wherein distinct times are apprehended all at once, as if from outside time (subcode tls.etr). The discussion so far has focused on the immediate experiential dimension of temporality -what the codebook calls "metacategory 1." But the ordinary baseline state also involves cognitive appraisals of and orientations to time (metacategory 2). Here, it is noted that the ordinary baseline contains tacit folk metaphysics of time: an intuitive, taken-for-granted realism that assumes time objectively flows towards an open future. Psychedelic states can transform these implicit assumptions into explicit metaphysical convictions or noetic insights (main code MPH). These may range from convictions that time or its passage is fundamentally illusory (subcode mph.unr), to beliefs about whether the future is predetermined and fated (subcode mph.fat), or appraisals concerning the nature of time itself (subcode mph.nat).

Figure 3. Non-inferiority of LLM-human relative to human-human agreement for each main code. Points show ΔAC1 (mean human-human AC1 minus mean LLM-human AC1); horizontal bars show paired-bootstrap 95% CIs from 2,000 resamples of the 247-unit validation sample. Positive values indicate human-human agreement higher than LLM-human agreement. The dashed line marks the +0.10 non-inferiority margin: all CI upper bounds fall below it, with RTD closest (+0.098). All code-specific mean LLM-human AC1 values also meet the prespecified 0.70 floor (not plotted). Alt text: A forest plot displaying the difference in AC1 agreement (human-human minus LLMhuman) with 95% bootstrap confidence interval error bars for seven main codes. A dashed vertical reference line at +0.10 marks the non-inferiority margin. All seven confidence intervals lie completely to the left of +0.10, confirming non-inferiority of LLM raters.

Figure 4.

Figure 4. Replicated co-occurrence complex and its stability across corpus history. (a) Positive code-pair associations surviving BH-FDR correction in both LLM coders (N = 3,291).

Alt text: Two-panel figure showing the associative structure of altered temporality. Panel (a) shows a network graph of nine robust positive co-occurrence edges linking flow structure (STF), standpoint relocation (REL), timelessness (TLS), metaphysical insight (MPH), social/narrative orientation (NSO), and loss of meaning (LMG), with MPH serving as a central hub and rate/duration distortion (RTD) disconnected. Panel (b) shows odds ratio point estimates across three historical calendar epochs, demonstrating persistent elevation for complex edges and independence for RTD edges.

Figure 5.

Figure 5. Cross-corpus reproduction of prevalence and association structure. (a) Maincode prevalence among filtered coded units in Shroomery (N = 3,291) and Neurogroove (N = 542), separately by coder. Codes are ordered by each coder's Shroomery prevalence. Filled slate-blue and amber markers show the observed Shroomery and Neurogroove estimates; hollow slate-blue markers show Shroomery prevalence standardized to Neurogroove's reportlength distribution using octile bins. (b) Pairwise association reproduction for the 16 of 21 code pairs meeting the measurability criterion (≥ 5 both-positive units in every coder-corpus matrix). Each point plots the Neurogroove log odds ratio against the corresponding samecoder Shroomery estimate; odds ratios use a uniform Haldane correction. Black markers denote the six measurable edges of the nine-edge co-occurrence complex identified in Figure 4, all positive in both corpora and both coders; the three unmeasurable edges (all involving REL) are omitted. Mid-grey markers denote RTD edges and light-grey markers the remaining measurable pairs. Alt text: Two-panel cross-corpus replication figure. Panel (a) compares main code prevalences between English (Shroomery) and Polish (Neurogroove) corpora across Claude Opus and GLM, showing consistent rank ordering and report-length standardization effects. Panel (b) is a scatter plot comparing pairwise log odds ratios in Neurogroove against Shroomery, demonstrating replication of the positive co-occurrence complex in the upper right quadrant and independent clustering of RTD around zero.
